# Problem and motivation

A neural network trained on one task and then on a second loses most of
what it learned first. A network that reaches 98% on handwritten digits
can fall to around 20% on those same digits after being trained on a
different task, and the loss happens within a few hundred gradient steps.
This failure is called catastrophic forgetting, and it has a simple cause:
the loss function minimised during the second task contains no term for
the first, so nothing in the optimisation preserves the earlier solution.

The practical consequence is that a deployed model cannot usually be
updated with new data. It has to be retrained on everything, which is
expensive and sometimes impossible when the original data has been deleted
or cannot be retained. Continual learning is the field that tries to
remove this constraint.

This note reports an experiment on how forgetting depends on the
similarity between two sequential tasks, and whether Elastic Weight
Consolidation protects the first task better than simple experience replay
as that similarity falls.

# Essential theoretical background

Forgetting follows from how gradient descent works. Training on Task B
minimises a loss defined only on Task B, so the shared weights are free to
move to whatever configuration suits B, and the configuration that solved
A is overwritten. Avoiding this means keeping the network stable enough to
retain the old solution while leaving it plastic enough to learn the new
one, a trade-off known as the stability-plasticity dilemma. Every method
in this study is one position on that trade-off.

# Relevant literature

Three findings are well established. @goodfellow2013 measured forgetting
systematically across activation functions and training algorithms, and
introduced the permuted-MNIST benchmark this study uses. @kirkpatrick2017
proposed EWC, which adds a quadratic penalty weighted by the diagonal
Fisher information, so that parameters important to the old task are
constrained while the rest stay free; they also showed that a uniform L2
penalty fails, because protecting every weight equally prevents the
network from learning the new task at all. Against both, simple experience
replay remains a strong baseline: @chaudhry2019tiny found plain replay
outperforming purpose-built continual-learning methods across four
benchmarks, and @hsu2018 report 95.19% for naive rehearsal against 91.04%
for EWC on domain-incremental permuted MNIST, with a plain L2 penalty
reaching 91.08%.

What remains unsettled is the relationship between task similarity and
forgetting. The intuitive expectation is monotonic: the less alike two
tasks are, the more is forgotten. Several studies report the opposite
pattern, with the most forgetting at intermediate similarity.
@ramasesh2021 observe this on interpolated CIFAR-10 task pairs and trace
it to the deeper layers of the network; @lee2021 derive it analytically in
a teacher-student setting and separate feature similarity from readout
similarity, finding that the two interact; @goldfarb2024 show that the
shape of the curve depends on how overparameterised the network is,
non-monotonic for a wide multilayer perceptron and monotonic near the
interpolation threshold, and note that earlier work reached no consensus
on the question. This disagreement is the gap the present experiment
addresses.

## Metrics

Let $R[i,j]$ be the test accuracy on task $j$ after training through task
$i$. With two tasks this is a $2\times2$ matrix, reported in full. From it
we compute average accuracy and backward transfer as defined by
@lopezpaz2017, and forgetting and intransigence as defined by
@chaudhry2018:

$$
\text{Forgetting} = R[1,1] - R[2,1], \qquad
\text{BWT} = R[2,1] - R[1,1],
$$

$$
\text{FWT} = R[1,2] - \bar{b}_2, \qquad
\text{Intransigence} = a^{*}_{2} - R[2,2],
$$

where $\bar{b}_2$ is the accuracy of the freshly initialised network on
Task B and $a^{*}_{2}$ is the Task B accuracy of the jointly trained
model. For two tasks forgetting and BWT are the same quantity with
opposite signs; both are reported so that the numbers are comparable to
either convention in the literature.

Every forgetting number is reported beside $R[2,2]$, the accuracy on Task
B. A sufficiently strong penalty can drive forgetting to zero simply by
preventing the network from learning Task B at all, and intransigence
measures exactly that cost.
